description: Hi! I'm Alexander, a 2nd-year Software Engineering student at Ural Federal University. I did a frontend internship at T1 Innotech: built mobile layouts, fixed critical bugs and made the UI for an HR chatbot. I'm into AI and computer vision, and I like shipping a working demo fast with clean UX. Looking for: a backend dev (Python/Node), an ML/data person and a designer or product-minded teammate. Fully committed for the whole hackathon - let's build something great!
summary: SPHEREx Blink is a free public web tool that turns NASA SPHEREx's all-sky infrared survey into a time-lapse of any patch of sky. You type coordinates or an object name. The tool fetches every SPHEREx exposure of that spot from NASA/IPAC IRSA, aligns them north-up on one pixel grid and plays them as a short animation, so a moving brown dwarf, nearby star, asteroid or comet jumps out at a glance. Difference images, deep stacks, false-colour images from SPHEREx's six detector arrays, a Gaia DR3 overlay placed at each frame's date, contamination-flag metadata and an on-the-fly spectrum and light curve help anyone, expert or not, confirm what they see. Views are shareable URLs and can be embedded in other sites. SPHEREx images over a billion objects every six months, far more than professionals can inspect alone. Tools like this let volunteers join the search, as they did with WISE and Backyard Worlds, where the public found most known brown dwarfs.
details:
WHAT IT DOES. The user enters Right Ascension and Declination in degrees or sexagesimal, or an object name. SPHEREx Blink shows every SPHEREx observation of that field as a blinking animation. There are two time scales: "Survey visits" gives one stacked frame per six-month pass (for stars and brown dwarfs), and "Every exposure" shows frames hours apart (for asteroids and comets). Display modes are Blink, Difference vs previous, Difference vs mean (static objects cancel, movers appear as bright/dark pairs) and Deep stack. Users choose the field of view (1.2 to 30 arcmin), which of the six detector arrays (0.75-5.0 micron) to stack, the stretch (asinh/log/sqrt/linear), and can build a false-colour RGB image from any three arrays.

HOW IT WORKS. A Python/FastAPI backend queries NASA/IPAC IRSA's IVOA SIA2 service for all SPHEREx Spectral Images containing the target, across the configured releases (DR1 and QR3 by default). It downloads small cutouts in parallel from IRSA's cutout service and caches them. For each exposure it subtracts the zodiacal-light model (ZODI extension) and masks defective pixels using the bit names in the FLAGS header, while keeping real-source flags. It then resamples every exposure onto one north-up gnomonic grid at SPHEREx's 6.15 arcsec pixel scale and coadds by inverse variance. For each exposure it also measures aperture photometry at the target and reads the exact wavelength from the spectral WCS, producing a spectrum and light curve on the fly, coloured by visit so variability is visible. The browser receives raw float frames, so contrast, colour and differencing changes are instant.

CHECKING DISCOVERIES. Gaia DR3 stars are drawn at their predicted position for each frame's date using their proper motions; fast movers get a five-year arrow, so an unexplained moving source stands out. An Aladin Lite panel shows WISE, 2MASS, DSS or Pan-STARRS imagery around the field. A frames table lists date, exposure count, arrays, coverage and the SPHEREx flags set at the target; flagged frames are marked.

SHARING AND UPDATES. Every view is a URL (?ra=...&dec=...&fov=...&view=..., or ?target=R+Dra); &embed=1 gives a bare player for other websites, and the animation can be saved as a video. The API is open (CORS) for notebooks. No data is stored locally: new SPHEREx observations appear as soon as IRSA publishes them, and a future release is a one-line configuration change.

TESTED ON the challenge targets: Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855-0714, RW Aurigae and R Draconis (one-click presets). Name lookups apply proper motion from J2000 to today; otherwise Barnard's Star, which has moved about 4 arcmin since 2000, would fall outside a small field. Automated tests on synthetic SPHEREx-format data confirm that after alignment a moving star is recovered at its predicted position and a fixed star stays put, both within 0.35 pixel.

TOOLS: Python, FastAPI, astropy, reproject, numpy, httpx; HTML/CSS/JavaScript (no framework); Aladin Lite v3; Docker.

IMPACT. Anyone with a browser can search SPHEREx for new nearby brown dwarfs, high proper-motion stars, moving Solar System objects and variable sources. We hope SPHEREx Blink can serve citizen science the way WiseView served Backyard Worlds.

USE OF AI: Much of the source code and documentation was generated and refactored with an AI coding assistant (Anthropic Claude) under the team's direction; the concept, design and data choices are the team's, and the code was reviewed and tested by the team. This is stated in the repository README and in the web page's generator meta tag. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used.
